analysis.one_liner: Boosts safety inspections, slows line speeds, and restricts abusive attendance policies in meat and poultry plants.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised safety protections for the roughly half a million people who work in meat and poultry plants. It would have funded new OSHA inspectors, stopped federal approval of faster slaughter line speeds unless independent safety review proved they would not hurt workers, required OSHA to set standards for repetitive-motion injuries and airborne disease, barred the point-based attendance systems that penalize workers for legally protected sick leave, and given workers stronger tools to sue over retaliation. It also would have restored country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy, limited large packers' use of spot-market livestock purchases, and conditioned federal grants to small processors on labor peace agreements.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers, who face injury, amputation, and repetitive-strain rates far above the private-sector average, along with the livestock farmers and ranchers who would gain bargaining protections against the handful of companies that buy their animals.

how_it_helps.text: The bill appropriates $60 million per year through FY2027 for additional OSHA inspectors and related enforcement, in an industry where enforcement has been thin relative to the injury rates.

It blocks the Agriculture Department from funding or approving line-speed increases at covered plants unless a federal safety official first certifies that higher speeds would not harm worker safety, and it freezes any policy that would increase line speeds during the covered period.

It makes it unlawful for employers to run no-fault, point-based attendance systems unless they clearly exempt legally protected leave (such as disability accommodations and family and medical leave), and gives workers a private right to sue for violations with damages and attorney's fees.

It requires OSHA to write standards for ergonomics and for preventing occupational exposure to COVID-19 and future airborne pathogens at meat and poultry plants, requires weekly public reporting of plant infections and deaths during pandemics, guarantees bathroom access without punishment, and strengthens retaliation protections, including a presumption of retaliation when an adverse action follows within 90 days of a safety complaint.

It restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and extends it to dairy, restricts large packers' spot-market purchases of livestock, allows attorney's fees under the Packers and Stockyards Act, and requires grantees of meat and poultry processing grants to sign labor peace agreements and not sell facilities to packers with more than 10 percent market share for 10 years.

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies, whose ability to run fast lines, penalize absences, and limit workers' legal leverage would be directly curtailed, and who would bear compliance, staffing, and inspection costs.

drawbacks.text: Slower line speeds, added inspection staffing, and attendance-policy rules raise meatpackers' operating costs, and packers would likely pass some of that through to consumers in meat prices.

The fair attendance policy subtitle is not limited to meatpacking: it applies to employers of 15 or more workers across the economy, which imposes recordkeeping and reporting burdens on many businesses well outside the industry the bill targets.

Mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork previously led to World Trade Organization rulings and retaliatory tariffs against the United States before it was repealed, so restoring it carried trade-dispute risk.

The bill gives workers a private right of action to sue over any OSHA violation at covered plants, bypassing the agency's usual enforcement discretion, which critics would call a broad expansion of litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-safety case is well documented in the bill's own findings: meat and poultry workers suffer double the private-industry amputation rate, musculoskeletal injuries that can exceed half the workforce, and documented harassment and retaliation. The main costs fall on the packing industry's operating model and potentially on meat prices, and a few provisions (economy-wide attendance rules, country-of-origin labeling's trade history) are real but secondary. On balance, the bill's benefits flow to a low-wage workforce while its costs fall on highly concentrated, profitable firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on November 30, 2021, and the committee never took it up again for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the bill on November 30, 2021, joined by four Democratic cosponsors and one Independent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward, through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies, whose line speeds, attendance systems, and market practices stayed exactly as they were, and who face no new inspection or labeling requirements.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed meatpacking worker safety, line speed limits, and anti-retaliation protections.

for.name: Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand, Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, and Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day of introduction; Sanders, the chamber's Independent, was the fifth cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 30, 2021, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies
against.role: Meat and poultry processors subject to the bill's line-speed, labeling, and labor provisions
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed line-speed restrictions and mandatory country-of-origin labeling, provisions of this type, in past rulemaking and industry campaigns; the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded floor fight.

sides.party_line_note: Every senator attached to the bill was a Democrat or the chamber's lone-aligned Independent (a sponsor, four of 48 Democrats, and one of two Independents); no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-majority committee never acted, so the bill died without any recorded vote.

industries.note: Line-speed freezes, mandatory OSHA ergonomic and airborne-pathogen standards, bathroom-access rules, curbs on no-fault attendance systems, retaliation protections, and a private right to sue all cut directly into the industry's low-cost, fast-line labor model. The industry's gain from the bill dying was keeping that model intact.

The bill would restrict spot-market livestock purchases, restore mandatory country-of-origin labeling, add attorney's fees for farmer suits under the Packers and Stockyards Act, and bar grant recipients from selling facilities to packers holding more than 10 percent market share. These provisions would erode the bargaining power of the small set of firms that dominate livestock buying.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers, poultry growers, and dairy farmers
industries.note: Country-of-origin labeling, limits on packer spot purchases, and attorney's fees under the Packers and Stockyards Act would give independent producers more transparency and leverage against the packers who buy their animals.

The bill would extend $100 million in processing-facility grants through FY2031 and fund local and regional food systems, directing public money toward smaller plants — though only on conditions (labor peace agreements, no sale to dominant packers) that keep the money from reaching the big firms.
